audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three quoted passages are present verbatim at the cited locators in the held files (Temple 1903 p. 115-116, scanned lines 19666-19668 with the p. 116 break and 'Balawa' paragraph visible; Zamponi & Comrie 2021 sec. 2.2 p. 22, lines 3063-3066; Portman 1898 p. 29, lines 1927-1932), and the Portman page image fetched sources today confirms the printed wording behind the scanned misreads. sources.citation: Portman, M. V. 1898. Notes on the Languages of the South Andaman Group of Tribes. Calcutta: Government Printing. Page images pp. 29-30 from archive.org (notesonlanguage00portgoog, leaves n43-n44).
sources.quote: 'A line is placed under a syllable to show the stress on it. When a word is not so marked the stress should be placed on the first syllable. In the vocabulary where words are used with hyphens or affixes, the ROOT is printed in italics.' Then Akar-Bale-specific notes: 'The Bálé language has a peculiar lingual, thick, t ... The long á with this tribe is always pronounced as if preceded by a very short o. O is the distinguishing vowel of the Bálé language'.
sources.note: Portman underlines stressed non-initial syllables word by word in Akar-Bale forms; the underlines are lost in the held scanned text layer. Inspecting the scans would give direct Akarbale evidence on whether long vowels attract stress off the root-initial syllable (Temple's claim) — the only language-specific stress data that exists. Two statement pages (29-30) fetched sources now; the vocabulary leaves were not.

sources.note: Only modern linguist-authored analysis of stress in a South Andamanese language, built on the same Portman 1898 underline-marked data that covers Akarbale; would show whether Temple 1903's 'every long vowel' weight clause (the sole basis of our QS-HEDGED/CVV coding) survives, or whether stress is simply root-initial as Z&C 2021 state family-wide (which would recode to morphological/root-initial).
